title: Face Detection — and a Word on Privacy
description: The same box-and-confidence idea, aimed at faces — plus an honest conversation about what that actually means.

content.value: Face detection uses exactly the same technique as last lesson's object detection — a box, a confidence score — just trained specifically to find faces, and often specific landmarks on them: eyes, nose, mouth corners.

content.title: 🔎 Detect the landmarks
content.hint: Same technique as object detection, aimed at a face this time.

content.value: It's worth being exact about what just happened: the model found where a face is, not whose face it is. Recognising a specific person is a separate, much more sensitive capability — one that raises real questions this course won't wave away.

A robot that can locate a face is one step from a robot that could track a specific person, store images of people who never agreed to it, or make decisions based on who it thinks someone is. None of that requires bad intentions — it can happen just from building a feature without thinking through who's affected. Anyone building with this technology has a responsibility to think about consent, storage, and who has access to what's captured, before deploying it.
This is a genuinely unresolved area of technology ethics, not a solved problem with one right answer — which is exactly why it's worth pausing on here rather than rushing past it.

Key takeaway: face detection finds where a face is, using the same technique as any other object detection. Detecting is not identifying — and any real use of this capability comes with genuine consent and privacy responsibilities.

quiz.question: What's the real difference between face detection and face identification?
options: There is no difference, they're the same thing
Detection finds where a face is; identification determines whose face it is — a separate, more sensitive capability
Identification is always less accurate than detection
quiz.explain: This lesson is careful to distinguish the two — detection alone says nothing about who is in the frame.

quiz.question: Why does this lesson raise privacy and consent explicitly?
options: Because face-related capabilities can affect real people who never agreed to being tracked or recorded, even without bad intent
It's a legal requirement with no real teaching purpose
Privacy isn't actually a real concern here
quiz.explain: Even a well-intentioned feature can affect people who never consented — that's exactly why this responsibility matters regardless of intent.
